text: Finding velocity and displacement from acceleration. Kinematic equations from integral calculus. In later chapters, we'll start with a force that depends on the acceleration A. There is some insight into why calculus is useful to determine or remember the kinematic equations. Let's begin with a particle with an acceleration A of T, which we can express in differential form by A of T equals DV of T over DT in terms of the velocity function. One way to solve a differential equation is to take the indefinite integral of both sides, where we get the integral of A of T with respect to T plus C sub 1 equals the integral of DV of T over DT with respect to T and C sub 1 represents a constant of integration. Note the integral of the derivative of a function is simply the function. For example, the integral of DF of X over DX with respect to X equals F of X. The integral is also called the anti-derivative because it is like an inverse operation of the derivative. This is similar to how the square root of X squared equals X if we take only the positive root. Using the anti-derivative property from calculus, we have the integral of A of T with respect to T plus C sub 1 equals V of T. We can employ the same procedure to write the velocity function in terms of the position function as V of T equals DX of T over DT. And with the integral we have the integral of V of T with respect to T plus C sub 2 equals X of T, where C sub 2 is a second constant of integration. Checkpoint. Pause and check your understanding. If acceleration is the slope of the velocity graph, what does the area under an acceleration versus time graph represent? Using these integrals we can derive the kinematic equations. Since A of T can be any function, let's assume that A of T equals A times T to the 0th power, which equals the constant A. Then we can evaluate the velocity function as V of T equals the integral of A with respect to T plus C sub 1, which equals V0 plus AT, where C sub 1 equals V0 equals V of 0. Then we can substitute into the integral to get the position function or X of T equals the integral of V0 plus AT with respect to T plus C sub 2, which equals X0 plus V0T plus 1 half AT squared, where C sub 2 equals X0 equals X of 0. Example problem. Motion of a motorboat. The problem. A motorboat is traveling at a constant velocity of 5.0 meters per second, when it begins to accelerate opposite the direction of motion to arrive at a dock. Its acceleration is A of T equals negative 1-quarter T meters per second cubed. Part A. What is the velocity function of the motorboat? Part B. At what time does the velocity reach 0? Part C. What is the position function of the motorboat? Part D. What is the displacement of the motorboat from the time it begins to decelerate to the time its velocity reaches 0? Part E. Graph the velocity and position functions. The model. The motorboat moves in one dimension along the direction of its initial motion. The acceleration is time dependent and points opposite the motion, so velocity is found by integrating acceleration and position is found by integrating velocity. We choose the initial position as the origin and measure time from the instant the deceleration begins. The math. Part A. Velocity is found by integrating the acceleration function with respect to time, which gives V of T equals the integral of A of T with respect to T, which equals the integral of negative 1-4-T with respect to T, and equals negative 1-8-T squared plus C sub 1. The integration constant is determined by the initial velocity V of 0 equals 5.0 meters per second, which gives C sub 1 equals 5.0 meters per second. The velocity function is therefore V of T equals 5.0 minus 1-8-T squared in meters per second. Part B. The stopping time occurs when the velocity reaches 0, so the velocity function gives 0 equals 5.0 minus 1-8-T squared. Solving this equation for the positive time gives T squared equals 40, T equals 6.3 seconds. Part C. Position is found by integrating the velocity function with respect to time, which gives X of T equals the integral of V of T with respect to T, which equals the integral of 5.0 minus 1-8-T squared with respect to T, and equals 5.0-T minus 1-24-T cubed plus C sub 2. The initial position is chosen to be X of 0 equals 0, so C sub 2 equals 0. The position function is therefore X of T equals 5.0-T minus 1-24-T cubed in meters. Part D. The displacement while the boat slows to rest is found by evaluating the position function at T equals 6.3 seconds, which gives X of 6.3 seconds. Equals 5.0 times 6.3 minus 1-24 times 6.3 cubed equals 21 meters. Part E. The velocity and position graphs are generated from the functions derived above. The velocity graph decreases to 0 at T equals 6.3 seconds, and the position graph reaches its maximum value at that same time. The conclusion. The motor boat's velocity function is V of T equals 5.0 minus 1-8-T squared in meters per second, and its position function is X of T equals 5.0-T minus 1-24-T cubed in meters. The velocity reaches 0 at 6.3 seconds after the boat has traveled 21 meters. The velocity graph crosses 0 at the same time that the position graph reaches its maximum.
